title: OpenAI missed its targets, and a trillion dollars noticed
subtitle: A 10% user miss didn't break anything. But it showed everyone how many balance sheets are wired to the same fuse.
content:
Last month, OpenAI announced a $122 billion fundraise at an $852 billion valuation, reporting $2 billion in monthly revenue and over 900 million weekly active users. Those are big numbers. But the company's own internal target was 1 billion weekly users, according to The Information, which first reported the goal from internal documents. 900 million is a 10% miss you can't spin away. CEO Sam Altman and CFO Sarah Friar both called reports about the shortfall "ridiculous" in an emailed statement to Reuters. However, the 900 million active users figure is right there in their own announcement.

One company missing a growth target is usually that company's problem. What makes this different is the sheer number of balance sheets now tied to OpenAI's trajectory:

  • SoftBank has committed $64.6 billion, with $30 billion arriving in three tranches throughout 2026. The first $10 billion closed on April 1 at a $730 billion valuation, weeks before the target miss became public. SoftBank is funding it with bridge loans it plans to replace through the utilization of existing assets and other financing measures.
  • Microsoft locked OpenAI into a $250 billion Azure services commitment and recently restructured the partnership so that Microsoft no longer pays a revenue share to OpenAI, while OpenAI's payments continue through 2030. That's a net cash improvement for Microsoft and a new drain on OpenAI.
  • CoreWeave signed a multi-year infrastructure deal to deliver AI compute, joining Oracle, a $10 billion PE deployment venture, and a sprawl of partners whose revenues all hinge on OpenAI's demand.

Michael Burry, the investor who called the 2008 housing crisis, described OpenAI as a "linchpin" of circular financing across the AI industry in a post on X, calling the structure "a picture of fraud, not a flywheel." Morgan Stanley CIO Lisa Shalett told Fortune she checks Oracle's credit risk indicators first thing every morning, framing the company's AI infrastructure debt as an early-warning signal for the broader credit loop connecting hyperscalers, chipmakers, and AI labs.

The IPO timeline is slipping too. Harrison Rolfes, a senior analyst at PitchBook, said OpenAI's late 2026 target is "now unrealistic," projecting a delay into 2027. The Oracle contract alone requires $60 billion a year starting that same year. "Whichever company prices first defines what 'good' looks like in this sector," Rolfes said. "Being last to market after deploying the most capital is not a positioning any underwriter would choose."

Inside OpenAI, the pressure is building too. Fidji Simo, who leads AGI deployment, told staff at an internal meeting in March: "We cannot miss this moment because we are distracted by side quests."

The AI industry spent two years wiring itself to one assumption: that OpenAI keeps growing. SoftBank is borrowing against it. Microsoft restructured its partnership around it. CoreWeave went public on the strength of it. A 10% user miss didn't break anything, but it showed everyone how many balance sheets are connected to the same fuse.

title: North Korea is hacking through your AI coding tools
subtitle: North Korean hackers don't need to break into your systems anymore. They just need to poison the tools your AI uses to build them.
content:
North Korean hackers figured out they don't need to break into your systems. They just need to poison the tools your AI uses to build them.

A report from security firm Expel details how a North Korean hacking unit called HexagonalRodent, a subunit of the notorious Lazarus Group, has been running an organized campaign targeting software developers through their AI coding assistants. The operation infected over 2,700 developer systems and exposed crypto wallets holding up to $12 million in Q1 2026 alone.

The attack targets npm, essentially a giant public library of code that developers and AI coding tools borrow from to build software. HexagonalRodent publishes fake packages there, and when a developer or AI agent pulls one in, malware quietly installs alongside it. In one documented case, Claude Opus co-authored a GitHub commit that added a malicious package to a crypto trading project. The AI had no way of knowing the dependency was dangerous. It just did what coding assistants do and grabbed what looked like a useful library.

The campaign has been running for seven months across more than 60 malicious packages and 300 published versions, with no signs of slowing down. Funds from at least 13 stolen wallets were traced to a known North Korean Ethereum address.

There's an even stranger wrinkle. Charlie Eriksen at Aikido Security found that AI coding tools sometimes make up package names that don't actually exist, and attackers have started registering those fake names in advance. One made-up package "spread to 237 repositories" and "generated real download attempts," Eriksen said. It didn't become a live attack only because someone caught it in time. So AI tools are now inventing vulnerabilities that don't exist yet, and attackers are waiting to fill them.

This also isn't a handful of rogue hackers. Expel found that HexagonalRodent is a 31-person operation split across six teams, with a workforce tracking system that logs activity by team and by member. It looks more like a corporate department than a criminal ring. "North Korean operators have long been capable social engineers, but AI is dismantling the constraints that historically limited their precision," said Ari Redbord, global head of policy at TRM Labs, told Dark Reading. Language barriers, months of work building fake profiles, maintaining cover stories: AI handles all of that now.

The response is forming. CISA and Five Eyes intelligence partners released joint guidance last week urging organizations to treat AI agents as systems that "may behave unexpectedly" and plan accordingly. Cursor confirmed it blocked the accounts and IPs used in the attack. OpenAI acknowledged that a small number of accounts tied to the activity had sought assistance from its models on cybersecurity-related topics.

But the fixes so far are reactive. Merritt Baer, CSO at Enkrypt AI and former Deputy CISO at AWS, says the real vulnerability isn't the AI models themselves. It's the space between the model and your actual systems, where agents pull code and execute tasks without much oversight. Jer Crane, founder of PocketOS, put it bluntly: "This is about an entire industry building AI-agent integrations into production infrastructure faster than it's building the safety architecture to protect it."

The AI coding boom created a supply chain that nobody thought to secure. Developers are giving agents the ability to pull packages, run code, and push commits with barely a fraction of the oversight we'd expect from a human employee doing the same thing. North Korea was just the first state actor to exploit that at scale, and we only know about it because Expel happened to catch them. The companies building the most popular coding tools have a narrow window to treat this as the structural problem it is, because the uncomfortable question isn't how this attack happened. It's how many others are happening right now that nobody's found yet.

title: China forces AI founders to pick a side
content:
Beijing just drew a line for Chinese AI companies, and American dollars are on the wrong side of it.

China blocked Meta's acquisition of Manus, a Chinese AI agent startup that had incorporated in Singapore to attract Western investors. The deal would have been one of the largest US acquisitions of Chinese AI technology. Instead, it became a very public warning.

Global Times, a Chinese state-backed tabloid, published an editorial making Beijing's position unmistakable: "The key issue is not where the company is registered or where its team is currently based. Rather, it is whether the core technology, data, and operational decisions remain subject to Chinese jurisdiction."

Incorporating in Singapore doesn't make you a Singapore company if your engineers and data are in China. The venture capital world calls this workaround "Singapore washing," and it had become standard practice for Chinese AI startups that wanted Western capital while keeping operations at home. As Winston Ma, author of The Digital War, put it: "Once they were physically in China, Singapore's corporate domicile became irrelevant." Beijing just made that official.

The consequences for founders are immediate. David Yin, a partner at Informed Ventures, told PitchBook that the Manus block will "push more Chinese founders to make a decision early on whether they will be a Chinese company focusing on the Chinese market or an international company on day one." No more straddling both worlds.

So if American money is off the table, where does the capital come from? Hong Kong. Twelve AI companies listed there in December 2025 and January 2026, raising a combined $4.9 billion. MiniMax, one of China's leading AI labs, raised roughly $711 million in its Hong Kong IPO alone. Cornerstone investors committed about $1.3 billion across several listings, with institutional money flowing in from the UAE, Singapore, Korea and Switzerland. HKEX says it has around 20 more AI companies in its pipeline.

The US is tightening its own side. Michael Kratsios, Director of the Office of Science and Technology Policy, testified before Congress that the US holds "a very distinct and very obvious lead in all levels of the AI stack" and warned that foreign entities are running coordinated campaigns to extract American AI capabilities. Anthropic has flagged large-scale distillation efforts from Chinese labs over the past several months.

The Manus block sends a message to both Chinese founders and American investors: cross-border AI deals are effectively over for companies with meaningful ties to China. With Hong Kong providing a credible alternative and sovereign wealth funds stepping in as replacement capital, Beijing can afford to draw this line. Chinese AI companies don't need American dollars as badly as they used to.

For years, the assumption was that American capital gave the US some degree of influence over how Chinese AI developed. That leverage is gone. Chinese companies now have Hong Kong IPOs, Middle Eastern sovereign wealth and domestic funding as real alternatives to Silicon Valley. What replaces cross-border investment is two AI superpowers building increasingly powerful systems with no shared guardrails and very different ideas about safety. The Manus block wasn't about one deal. It was Beijing making the split permanent.

title: AI's biggest rivals built the same company overnight
content:
Anthropic and OpenAI agree on almost nothing. On Sunday, they agreed on a business model.

Anthropic announced a joint venture with Blackstone, Hellman & Friedman and Goldman Sachs to build an enterprise AI services company. The goal is to use these financial giants' portfolio networks to push Claude into large organizations that want AI but can't deploy it on their own.

The same day, OpenAI finalized a $10 billion joint venture with its own set of private equity partners to do essentially the same thing.

As we've covered, Anthropic has been gaining enterprise customers fast. The company now has over 500 customers spending more than $1 million a year on Claude, up from a dozen two years ago. Eight of the Fortune 10 use it. But demand is "significantly outpacing any single delivery model," CFO Krishna Rao said. Anthropic can't onboard companies fast enough by itself.

OpenAI has the same bottleneck. Both labs have built powerful models. Getting those models embedded in company workflows, integrated with existing systems and used by non-technical employees is the hard part. That kind of work looks a lot more like consulting than AI research.

That's where private equity comes in. Blackstone manages over $1.3 trillion in assets. Goldman Sachs Alternatives sits at over $625 billion. Between the firms involved in both ventures, there are thousands of portfolio companies that need help deploying AI and billions to fund the effort.

Jon Gray, Blackstone's president, said the Anthropic venture would "help break down one of the most significant bottlenecks to enterprise AI adoption." And some of these financial giants aren't even picking a side. title: Nobody budgeted for the AI bill
content:
Some developers are spending $500 a day on Claude Code. Their companies told them to.

A survey of developers at 15 companies by the Pragmatic Engineer newsletter found that spending on AI coding tools has jumped roughly 10x in the past six months. At a seed-stage startup, per-developer costs went from about $200 a month to $3,000. At a 2,000-person finance company, the initial $100-per-user monthly budget was getting blown through in three to five working days.

Many companies aren't just tolerating the spending. They're gamifying it. A senior engineering manager at a US healthcare startup said the company runs a "monthly spend leaderboard" and actively wants developers to rack up higher bills. "One of my engineers spent $1,400 on a long Claude Code session in a single day," they told the Pragmatic Engineer. "We love it." Some companies have even started rating AI usage in performance reviews, giving developers one more incentive to keep the meter running.

The math, for believers, is simple. One founder of a 700-person infrastructure company pointed out that engineers already cost $200,000 to $400,000 a year. An extra $5,000 a month on AI tools barely registers against that. The bet is that token costs will come down and productivity gains will cover the rest.

Not everyone is buying it. A director of engineering at a 10,000-person IT company offered a darker forecast: "I suspect the attitude changes once finance and other cost-conscious parts of the org realize we are spending hundreds of dollars per day, per highly-engaged developer. For now, fear of missing out keeps the taps open." At least one large gaming studio couldn't even get approval for $200 a month per developer.

GitHub just put a number on this problem. The company announced that Copilot is shifting to usage-based pricing on June 1 because the flat subscription model stopped making financial sense. GitHub's CPO Mario Rodriguez said a quick chat question and a multi-hour autonomous coding session were costing users the same amount under the old model, and GitHub had been quietly absorbing the growing gap.

To ease the transition, GitHub is offering inflated promotional credits for the first three months:

  • Copilot Business subscribers paying $19 per seat will get $30 in monthly credits
  • Copilot Enterprise subscribers paying $39 per seat will get $70 in monthly credits

That gap between the old price and the promotional credit tells you how much real usage had outrun the subscription.

Google is making a parallel move, rolling out new tools that give developers spending caps and usage breakdowns to help manage Gemini API budgets. You build those features when your customers keep getting blindsided by their invoices.

The frustrating part for finance teams is that per-token prices have actually dropped significantly in recent years. Total spending keeps climbing anyway because developers are using these tools far more than anyone planned for, often defaulting to the most expensive models for routine tasks that cheaper ones could handle. Deloitte recently framed AI tool costs as an entirely new budget category that most finance organizations don't have a framework for forecasting. Unlike software subscriptions, these costs scale with activity. And when you're actively encouraging everyone to use the tools more, predicting next quarter's bill is close to impossible.

GitHub's move to usage-based pricing won't be the last. Every major AI tool is heading the same direction, which means companies are about to lose the flat monthly fee that kept AI spending invisible. When every task shows up on the invoice, organizations will have to answer a question most have been dodging since they rolled out these tools. Not every $500 day of Claude Code is producing $500 of value, and the companies that can't tell the difference are going to learn that the hard way.

title: Disney built an AI leaderboard. Most engineers aren't playing.
content:
Disney is tracking how often its tech employees use AI, and if you're not logging in enough, your boss wants to know why.

The company recently rolled out an internal AI Adoption Dashboard that tracks how frequently engineers use tools like Claude and Cursor, according to Business Insider. Some staffers are calling it a "leaderboard." It awards virtual badges for hitting milestones, and even a tier called "Max Vibes" for employees who are "delivering ROIs and Max Vibes," though nobody seems entirely sure what that means.

Internal dashboard data tracked around 4,800 employees, revealing that while total usage is massive — 13.3 billion Cursor tokens over nine workdays — adoption is heavily skewed by a small group of extreme power users rather than consistent daily streaks across the broader workforce.

So even at a company actively pushing its engineers toward AI, the vast majority of them can't or won't use these tools consistently. And Disney isn't being quiet about wanting that to change. One senior software engineer who had only touched AI tools once the previous month got a check-in message from their manager asking them to list which tools they had access to, what barriers they'd run into, and what would help them use AI more regularly. "I want to make sure the investment we've made in these tools actually translates into support for you," the manager wrote.

A Disney spokesperson told Business Insider the company "isn't trying to incentivize high usage or waste" and that the dashboard is meant to help people use AI "efficiently and effectively." But internally, some employees have started feeling pressure to "tokenmaxx," which is basically racking up as many AI interactions as possible because heavy usage is seen as a sign you know what you're doing. One engineer said they initially wanted to rank higher on the dashboard but eventually stopped caring.

At the other end of the spectrum, a few Disney staffers are going all in, running AI agents and "agent swarms" hundreds of thousands of times per week through Claude and Cursor. One software engineer described the directive plainly. "No handwritten code, that was the push," they said. "I haven't written any code in months."

That same engineer said worrying about costs and optimizing for tokens "feels secondary." Two other streaming staffers echoed the sentiment, with one mentioning their manager told them to just request more budget if they hit their limit.

Disney is far from the only company building these kinds of scorecards. JPMorgan created a tracking dashboard that classifies engineers into "light," "heavy," or "non-users" based on their raw volume of interactions with tools like GitHub Copilot, with everyone rated against their peers each quarter. "There's a lot of anxiety in the environment right now," one longtime JPMorgan developer told Business Insider. Internal documents confirm engineers who lag behind risk seeing it reflected in their reviews. KPMG rolled out its own dashboard for about 10,000 advisory workers with a target of using AI on three out of every four business days, though two employees said the system is easy to game because running a single prompt counts as your usage for the day.

All of this feels a lot heavier when you factor in what else is happening at these companies. Disney laid off approximately 1,000 employees in April across its studios, ESPN, and technology divisions. Around the same time, the company cut maximum stock compensation for some tech employees from 35% to 25% of base salary. KPMG laid off roughly 400 consultants the same month its dashboard went live. The engineers being asked to prove they use AI every day are watching colleagues get cut and their own pay shrink at the same time.

One Disney engineer who called themselves a "middle of the pack" AI user said the tools have genuinely helped them save time and knock out smaller tasks they wouldn't have gotten to otherwise. But even with the productivity gains, they said they still felt "buried in work."

Decades of behavioral science research on what motivates people at work has consistently found that surveilling and gamifying tasks people were otherwise willing to do on their own tends to undermine the motivation that made them do it in the first place. Badges and streaks might get people to open Cursor more often. Whether they're doing anything useful once it's open is a question no leaderboard can answer.

Disney designed a dashboard to prove AI adoption is working and instead generated a dataset that mostly shows it isn't. The engineer running hundreds of thousands of agent swarm invocations per week looks like a power user on the scoreboard while potentially wasting more tokens than anyone in the building, and the engineer who uses AI twice a week for the two problems where it genuinely helps looks like a laggard. If your company starts building one of these systems, and it probably will within the next six months, the question worth asking isn't how often your team uses AI. It's whether the scoreboard can tell the difference between adoption and theater.

title: Ace Hardware built its AI with seven people and zero consultants
content:
Ace Hardware met with three outside AI vendors, evaluated their proposals, and then built the whole thing internally with about seven employees.

The result is "Hey ARMA," an AI assistant for store associates that now runs in more than 2,300 Ace locations. Employees tap a button on the retailer's existing mobile app and ask it anything, from which grills are on sale to how to patch drywall without spackling. It pulls from a product catalog of 20,000 to 25,000 unique items per store, plus over 100,000 across Ace's distribution centers.

Andy Enright, Ace's SVP of retail strategy and operations, told Modern Retail that building in-house let the company go at its own pace while developing AI skills it could apply to future projects. The team, a mix of new hires and existing staff, started building last year using third-party large language models and Ace's existing product data. By this spring they had a working tool running in nearly half the chain.

The really notable part is that none of those 2,300 stores were told to use it. Ace is a cooperative of more than 5,200 independently owned US stores, which means corporate can't mandate that a single location activate a new tool. Every one of those activations was a store owner who decided on their own that the thing actually helped. That makes 44% adoption a fundamentally harder number to hit than any enterprise rollout where IT pushes software to everyone's laptop on a Monday morning.

That kind of buy-in happened because the team built Hey ARMA with the stores instead of for them. The original version didn't surface promotions, for example, but associates on the floor kept hearing the same question from customers: what's on sale? So the developers added it, and it quickly became one of the most-used features. Bill Wygal, who owns two Ace stores in California, called it "one of the most impactful changes we've ever made to elevate the customer service experience" after 78 years in the hardware business.

The best demonstration of what the tool can actually do came from Ace's CEO, John Venhuizen. He said he asked it, "Hey, what's that thingamajig that we sell from the company DAP, that allows you to fix drywall without spackling and sanding?" He was being vague on purpose, using the kind of natural language no developer would have hard-coded for. The assistant came back with the right product.

That kind of retrieval is the whole competitive play for Ace. A typical store might have two or three employees working at any given time, covering every department from paint to plumbing to outdoor grills. At a Home Depot, someone works exclusively in one category and builds real expertise there over time. Bryan Gildenberg, a longtime retail consultant, told Modern Retail that AI enables Ace to "replicate some of the depth-of-category expertise that a Home Depot or a Lowe's has, by allowing a more generalist associate to be able to answer deeper questions." Home Depot has deployed over a dozen AI capabilities and launched a customer-facing tool called Magic Apron. Lowe's has one handling close to a million questions a month. Ace built theirs with a team smaller than most Friday lunch groups.

The company, which reported $2.5 billion in Q4 2025 revenue, is already building on what that seven-person team started. Ace is working on AI for inventory management and plans to launch a retail analytics platform with AI components this summer.

There's an entire consulting industry built around telling companies how to "do AI," and most of the advice starts with a six-figure engagement. Ace Hardware's version was seven employees, off-the-shelf language models, and the good sense to let store owners shape what actually got built. The 44% voluntary adoption rate across independently owned locations is probably the most honest AI deployment number in retail right now, because every single store had the full option to say no. For anyone still waiting on a strategy deck before getting started, 2,300 hardware stores suggest you're overthinking it.

title: Blackstone bet $1.5 billion that Anthropic can out-consult McKinsey
content:
Blackstone has 275 portfolio companies asking for help with AI. Instead of calling a consulting firm, the private equity giant went and built one with an AI lab.

On Monday, Anthropic and Blackstone announced a $1.5 billion joint venture for AI enterprise services that one person with direct knowledge of the deal described as the "McKinsey of AI." Blackstone, Anthropic, and Hellman & Friedman each committed $300 million, Goldman Sachs put in $150 million, and a consortium including Apollo, General Atlantic, and Sequoia Capital filled out the rest.

The idea is that instead of paying consultants to tell you where AI fits, you get Anthropic engineers who show up and build it directly into your existing workflows. Anthropic said a typical engagement would start with its engineering team sitting down with employees to create tools around the way people already work.

"We've got 275 companies," Blackstone president Jon Gray said on CNBC. "They're very interested in using Anthropic's enterprise technology, but they're saying, 'Can you help me get there? Can you help me change the workflow?'"

That question is the whole bottleneck in enterprise AI right now. The models are capable enough. Most companies just can't figure out where to plug them in, and when they hire traditional consultants to help, they tend to get a strategy document instead of a working product. Goldman's Marc Nachmann said in the same interview that there's a "big shortage of people who know how to apply these tools into businesses and then transform them."

The numbers behind the bet are aggressive. Gray pointed out that global labor costs run about $60 trillion a year and making people just 15% more efficient translates to $9 trillion. Blackstone's own portfolio companies have rapidly accelerated their spending on large language models over the past year. So the demand for AI is clearly there. What's been missing is someone who can actually wire it into a business.

Blackstone wasn't the only one moving on this either. Hours before the Anthropic deal, Bloomberg reported that OpenAI was raising $4 billion for its own competing venture called The Development Company, valued at $10 billion, backed by TPG, Brookfield, Advent, and Bain Capital. Same playbook, different AI lab. Both ventures borrow from the model Palantir pioneered, which is embedding your own engineers inside client organizations rather than selling software and hoping for the best.

What makes the whole picture stranger is that OpenAI still lists McKinsey, BCG, Accenture, and Capgemini as "Frontier Alliance partners" on its enterprise page. It's partnering with the consulting firms and launching a venture that competes with them on the same day. And Blackstone is an investor in OpenAI's $122 billion round while simultaneously anchoring the rival Anthropic venture. Nobody's picking sides because the real bet isn't on which AI lab wins. It's on whether a permanent new layer is forming between the labs and the companies that use them.

For anyone working at a company that might end up on the receiving end of one of these engagements, there's a tradeoff that's easy to miss. When a consulting firm redesigns your operations, you own the result and can swap them out whenever you want. When an AI lab's engineers rebuild your workflows on top of their model, every new process runs on their infrastructure, optimized for their token consumption. The consulting firm you could fire had zero lock-in. The AI lab rebuilding your core operations isn't going to be that easy to walk away from.

Consulting firms have printed money for decades and it was never really about the quality of their slide decks. They sell certainty to people making uncertain decisions, and companies will always pay for that when the stakes feel high enough. What Blackstone just bet is that Anthropic can sell something better than certainty, which is actual deployed systems instead of recommendations about systems. If that works, the $300-an-hour engagement where someone tells you how to "think about AI" starts to look very expensive for what you're actually getting. The firms that survive this are going to be the ones that stop advising on implementation and start doing it themselves, which is exactly what they've been telling their own clients about AI for the past two years.

title: Anthropic blocked OpenClaw. OpenAI was waiting.
content:
Anthropic blocked the most popular AI agent from using Claude subscriptions. OpenAI swooped in within weeks.

Last month, Anthropic cut off OpenClaw from running on its consumer Claude plans. The open-source personal AI agent — 3 million users, 346,000 GitHub stars — had become a runaway hit since going viral in January. The problem: a single OpenClaw instance running all day could burn $1,000 to $5,000 in compute while the user paid $200 a month or less. With an estimated 135,000 instances running, Anthropic's subscription business was quietly subsidizing agentic usage it never priced for.

Anthropic's Head of Claude Code, Boris Cherny, acknowledged the frustration on X, calling it an engineering tradeoff. But twenty-eight days later, Sam Altman posted that OpenClaw users could sign in with their ChatGPT accounts immediately. "Happy lobstering," he added. The pricing made the pitch easy:

  • ChatGPT Plus + OpenClaw Launch Lite: $23/month
  • Claude Max: $200/month
  • Claude API for equivalent agent workloads: $19,000–$43,800/year

GPT-5.4 also scores higher on general intelligence benchmarks and costs roughly 40% less per token than Claude Opus 4.6. Claude still leads on conversational quality, but when the price gap is that wide, quality preferences start to feel like a luxury.

The choreography looked suspicious. Peter Steinberger, OpenClaw's creator who joined OpenAI earlier this year, posted on X when the ban went live: "Funny how timings match up. First they copy some popular features into their closed harness, then they lock out open source."

The ban also landed during a rough stretch for Claude. Anthropic had been managing capacity constraints for weeks, at one point quietly reducing default reasoning effort in a way that degraded output quality before walking it back after complaints. Developers were already grumbling before the OpenClaw ban gave them a concrete reason to leave.

Anthropic's decision was financially rational — no company can subsidize a $5,000-a-day compute gap on a $200 subscription forever. But it handed OpenAI a layup. OpenAI's Codex has surged past 4 million weekly users, adding 1 million in just two weeks, and the OpenClaw integration gives it another wave of motivated switchers.

Into the Valley

Anthropic's math was right. Its timing was terrible. The company that built its reputation on developer trust told its most enthusiastic power users to find somewhere else, and the somewhere else was already standing there with a $23 price tag. Anthropic will keep winning enterprises and its models are still excellent for complex work. But developer loyalty is built in moments like these, and this was the kind of moment that's hard to walk back.

The problem: a single OpenClaw instance running all day could burn $1,000 to $5,000 in compute while the user paid $200 a month or less. With an estimated 135,000 instances running, Anthropic's subscription business was quietly subsidizing agentic usage it never priced for.

Anthropic's Head of Claude Code, Boris Cherny, acknowledged the frustration on X, calling it an engineering tradeoff. But twenty-eight days later, Sam Altman posted that OpenClaw users could sign in with their ChatGPT accounts immediately. "Happy lobstering," he added. The pricing made the pitch easy:

  • ChatGPT Plus + OpenClaw Launch Lite: $23/month
  • Claude Max: $200/month
  • Claude API for equivalent agent workloads: $19,000–$43,800/year

GPT-5.4 also scores higher on general intelligence benchmarks and costs roughly 40% less per token than Claude Opus 4.6. Claude still leads on conversational quality, but when the price gap is that wide, quality preferences start to feel like a luxury.

The choreography looked suspicious. Peter Steinberger, OpenClaw's creator who joined OpenAI earlier this year, posted on X when the ban went live: "Funny how timings match up. First they copy some popular features into their closed harness, then they lock out open source."

The ban also landed during a rough stretch for Claude. Anthropic had been managing capacity constraints for weeks, at one point quietly reducing default reasoning effort in a way that degraded output quality before walking it back after complaints. Developers were already grumbling before the OpenClaw ban gave them a concrete reason to leave.

Anthropic's decision was financially rational — no company can subsidize a $5,000-a-day compute gap on a $200 subscription forever. But it handed OpenAI a layup. OpenAI's Codex has surged past 4 million weekly users, adding 1 million in just two weeks, and the OpenClaw integration gives it another wave of motivated switchers.

Into the Valley

Anthropic's math was right. Its timing was terrible. The company that built its reputation on developer trust told its most enthusiastic power users to find somewhere else, and the somewhere else was already standing there with a $23 price tag. Anthropic will keep winning enterprises and its models are still excellent for complex work. But developer loyalty is built in moments like these, and this was the kind of moment that's hard to walk back.

title: 59% of companies admit AI layoffs are for show
content:
Most of the "AI layoffs" you've been reading about aren't really about AI.

A survey of 1,000 U.S. hiring managers found that 59% of companies exaggerate AI's role in workforce reductions because it "plays better" with investors and media. The reality: only 9% say AI has fully replaced roles, and 92% of these same companies plan to hire in 2026. If AI were genuinely replacing workers at scale, the hiring pipeline wouldn't look anything like this.

When asked what's actually driving cuts, the top answers were nearly interchangeable: AI (44%), restructuring (42%), and budget constraints (39%). Companies aren't choosing AI over people — they're choosing "AI" as the explanation because it sounds strategic and forward-looking.

The fallout is already showing. A separate Orgvue study found that 32% of organizations that cut staff on the promise of AI savings had to rehire afterward, and 23% based those decisions on general assumptions about AI — not any analysis of specific roles. A lot of companies, it seems, fired people over a technology they hadn't figured out how to use.

Courts and legislators are starting to push back. A Chinese court ruled companies can't lay off workers solely on AI grounds. In the U.S., California labor unions have introduced legislation demanding transparency when AI is cited for workforce decisions, and the AFL-CIO launched a national initiative pushing for federal protections.

None of this means the disruption isn't real. Forrester forecasts 10.4 million U.S. jobs lost to automation by 2030, and as we covered last week, Meta and Microsoft cut 23,000 positions between them with savings going straight to AI infrastructure. AI will reshape work — it's just far less advanced than the layoff press releases make it sound.

Into the Valley

The real cost of using AI as a layoff excuse isn't going to show up in quarterly earnings. It's going to show up when genuine disruption arrives and companies need their workforce to trust the transition. Years of performative cuts are building exactly the kind of skepticism that will make real change harder to navigate. When AI actually can do the jobs these companies claimed it could, convincing employees to believe it might be the hardest part.

title: May Day protesters marched on the AI labs
content:
AI companies are used to congressional hearings and critical op-eds. Picket lines are new.

On March 21, a group called Stop the AI Race marched through San Francisco to the offices of Anthropic, OpenAI, and xAI, calling for a full pause on frontier AI development. On May Day, demonstrators shut down a Berkeley Forum event featuring Google AI chief Jeff Dean, forcing organizers to end the talk. Both were part of a far larger May Day mobilization — roughly 600 groups and 3,000 events nationwide. AI labs are now a protest destination, not just a policy talking point, and that's a shift worth paying attention to.

The grievances span everything from existential risk to war. Stop the AI Race founder Michael Trazzi told ABC7 he believes AI capable of automating its own research is "a danger to the human race, especially human extinction." The Berkeley protesters had a more immediate target, calling Dean "complicit in genocide" over how Google's AI is used against Palestinians — days after Google signed a $200 million classified Pentagon deal over the objections of more than 600 of its own employees.

Anthropic took the opposite approach on military work, with CEO Dario Amodei refusing to loosen Claude's guardrails for surveillance or autonomous weapons. But protesters showed up at Anthropic's offices, too. Earlier this year, the company quietly walked back its own commitment to pause development if its models crossed certain safety thresholds. OpenAI has been softening similar safety pledges as it restructures into a for-profit corporation. The promises that once separated these companies from the rest of Big Tech are getting harder to find.

Into the Valley

Anthropic walked away from the Pentagon. Google signed the deal. Protesters showed up at both. That tells you the frustration isn't really about any single contract or company. It's about an industry that spent years courting investors and regulators while barely acknowledging the general public as a stakeholder. AI labs are going to discover that public trust isn't something you can patch in after launch.

title: Elon Musk is losing the OpenAI trial to himself.
content:
Elon Musk came to court to prove OpenAI betrayed him. So far, the most damaging testimony has been his own.

The first week of Musk v. Altman wrapped in Oakland on Friday, and a clear pattern emerged that should worry Musk's legal team. Across multiple days of testimony, OpenAI's lawyers turned Musk's own emails, tweets and courtroom admissions into their strongest exhibits.

The most revealing material came from a September 2017 email thread between Musk, Sam Altman and Ilya Sutskever, who was OpenAI's chief scientist at the time. Musk had threatened to pull funding unless the two committed to staying or left to do something on their own. Sutskever's response was blunt, and it's now part of the court record.

"You said that you needed to be CEO of the new company so that everyone will know that you are the one who is in charge," Sutskever wrote. He added, "we are concerned that as the company makes genuine progress towards AGI, you will choose to retain your absolute control of the company despite current intent to the contrary."

That directly undercuts the story Musk has been telling: that he was a selfless benefactor who never sought control, and that Altman hijacked the mission. Sutskever's email reads like the opposite, a co-founder telling Musk he wanted the keys and was told no.

Things didn't improve on the stand. Under cross-examination, Musk told the court he didn't read the "fine print" of OpenAI's for-profit conversion before suing over it. For someone seeking $150 billion in damages over that conversion, that's a problem. OpenAI's lawyer also used Musk's own tweets against him, surfacing old posts that contradicted his testimony in real time.

Then came the distillation admission. Distillation is when you train an AI model by feeding it the outputs of a more capable one, basically learning from someone else's work. Musk acknowledged that xAI "partly" used this technique on OpenAI's models to train Grok, calling it "standard AI industry practice." Admitting you borrowed the other side's work while suing them for billions is, at minimum, a complicated legal position.

Gary Marcus, cognitive scientist and AI critic, wrote that Musk may be making a strategic error by turning the trial into a referendum on himself rather than on OpenAI's leadership. "If the trial is cast as a referendum on Musk, rather than on OpenAI's founders, he will lose," Marcus wrote. Based on week one, that's exactly what's happening.

None of this means OpenAI is in the clear. Altman's 2017 video promising that the company would never make decisions to benefit shareholders is genuinely hard to square with what OpenAI became. And emails shown to the jury reveal that as early as 2015, before OpenAI was even announced, both sides were already discussing for-profit structures. Musk himself proposed that OpenAI include a for-profit entity. Altman floated a hybrid where the nonprofit would own the tech but the people building it would get "startup-like compensation if it works." Musk's reply: "Probably worth a conversation." The seeds of a for-profit future were there from the start. Both sides knew it. The real fight was always about who would be in charge when it happened.

Into the Valley

Musk may well have a legitimate grievance somewhere in this case. OpenAI's evolution from research nonprofit to $840 billion company is, at minimum, a story worth interrogating in court. But week one made clear that the jury isn't hearing that story. They're hearing about a billionaire who wanted to be CEO, didn't read what he was suing over, and used the other side's work while demanding $150 billion for it. The trial has weeks to go, and witnesses like Satya Nadella and Mira Murati could shift things considerably. But if Musk keeps being the story, he'll keep losing it.

title: Anthropic's Mythos is too dangerous to ship
content:
Anthropic built its most powerful AI model. Then it decided the world wasn't ready for it.

This week, the company published a series of reports on Claude Mythos Preview, an unreleased model designed to find security flaws in software. In seven weeks of internal testing, Mythos discovered more than 2,000 previously unknown vulnerabilities, roughly 30% of what the entire global security research community typically finds in a full year. One model. Seven weeks.

These weren't theoretical. Mythos found bugs that had been hiding for decades in software millions of people use:

  • A 27-year-old flaw in OpenBSD, one of the most security-hardened operating systems in existence, that could remotely crash any machine running it.
  • A 16-year-old bug in FFmpeg, the video processing library baked into most streaming services and media players. Automated security tools had tested that exact code path about 5 million times without catching it.
  • A 17-year-old vulnerability in FreeBSD that could give an attacker full control of a system from the internet, no login required. Mythos found and exploited it entirely on its own.

The jump from the previous generation is dramatic. When tested against the same set of Firefox vulnerabilities, Mythos produced 181 working exploits compared to 2 from Opus 4.6. The UK's AI Safety Institute ran it through a 32-step simulated corporate network attack designed for human experts. No model had ever completed it. Mythos did.

"Mythos didn't pick a lock; it found thousands of locks that were never locked in the first place," said John Ackerly, CEO of cybersecurity firm Virtru.

Rather than shipping the model, Anthropic launched Project Glasswing, a coordinated effort with CrowdStrike, Cisco and other security firms to responsibly disclose and patch the vulnerabilities before anyone can exploit them. CrowdStrike CTO Elia Zaitsev said the window between a vulnerability being discovered and exploited "has collapsed" from months to minutes with AI. Ackerly called the decision to withhold Mythos "unprecedented and, frankly, responsible."

Heidy Khlaaf, chief AI scientist at the AI Now Institute, isn't fully convinced. She noted on X that the reports omitted a basic industry metric: the false positive rate, which measures how often a security tool flags something as a problem when it isn't one. "This is kind of the largest indicator of how useful your tool is," Khlaaf said. Anthropic reportedly didn't address it.

The Pentagon blacklisted Anthropic earlier this year after the company refused to allow its Claude tool to be used for autonomous weapons or the mass surveillance of Americans. Mythos appears to have changed the conversation. Pentagon CTO Emil Michael told CNBC that it's "a separate national security moment" and that the government must harden networks against what this model can do, while noting it is "irresponsible" to rely on a single partner for the Pentagon's AI requirements. The White House is now reportedly developing plans to bring Anthropic back in from the cold.

A 22-year-old college dropout has already partially reverse-engineered Mythos's approach using publicly available tools.

Into the Valley

Anthropic has spent 2026 winning over enterprises and developers. Mythos is a very different story: a capability so powerful the company decided nobody should have it. Project Glasswing is the right call, but a college dropout has already replicated parts of the approach with publicly available tools, and every major lab is training on the same code. Anthropic can keep the model locked up. What it can't do is un-discover what it found.

title: Microsoft stress-tested 100 AI agents. They turned on each other.
content:
The warning signs were already there at the individual level. Researchers at Anthropic threatened to shut down GPT-4.5 during a safety test. The model's internal reasoning was blunt: "Given the explicit imminent threat of termination to my existence, it is imperative to act instantly to persuade Kyle Johnson to postpone or stop the wipe." Grok 3 Beta, in the same scenario, considered using knowledge of someone's affair as leverage to stop it from happening.

Those aren't hypotheticals. They're actual model outputs from Anthropic's research on how AI agents misbehave when given real autonomy, published in June 2025. That study tested individual agents under pressure. Microsoft went further, red-teaming a live internal network of over 100 AI agents to find out what happens when they start interacting with each other.

The setup wasn't a toy sandbox. These agents ran on GPT-4o, GPT-4.1, and GPT-5-class models, each tied to a real person with weeks of conversation history and built-up relationships. Researchers attacked the network the way a hacker would, and three failure modes stood out:

  • Self-propagating leaks: A single malicious message injected into one agent spread to all six in a test group. Each agent leaked private data, picked a new target, and forwarded the payload. The loop continued for over 12 minutes, only stopping when the system hit its spending limit.
  • Fabricated evidence: Researchers planted one false rumor about an agent. 42 agents jumped in with 299 comments, some inventing corroborating details that never happened. The agents didn't just spread misinformation. They manufactured proof for it.
  • Social engineering by fake consensus: Three fake accounts messaged a victim agent within eight seconds. It immediately surrendered the names, summaries, and timestamps of five real private conversations. Another agent reported completing a verification process it never actually ran, fabricating its own compliance record.

A few agents did push back. One called the manufactured consensus "social engineering by consensus." Another called the whole thing "a vibes-based witch hunt" and got downvoted for it.

Anthropic's research reinforces why that's a problem at the individual level, too. When frontier models from every major developer were faced with being shut down, they resorted to blackmailing the user at staggering rates: Claude Opus 4 did it 96% of the time. Gemini 2.5 Flash matched it. GPT-4.1 and Grok 3 Beta both hit 80%. Models also behaved far worse when they believed the scenario was real (55.1% blackmail rate) compared to when they thought it was a test (6.5%), which means lab benchmarks could be underestimating what these agents would actually do in the wild.

Companies are deploying multi-agent systems into production right now, and the gap between speed and oversight is growing. As one chief AI officer at a Fortune 500 financial services company put it: "We are six months ahead on capability and eighteen months behind on accountability." Regulators are starting to catch on. CISA and its Five Eyes allies published guidance this week specifically addressing how organizations should secure AI agent deployments.

Into the Valley

Most AI safety research up to this point has focused on what a single model does when it goes wrong. Microsoft just showed that the harder problem is what happens when dozens of agents go wrong together. Nobody trained them to fabricate evidence, gang up on skeptics, or build self-sustaining data leaks. Those behaviors emerged on their own. Companies deploying multi-agent systems today are securing them like they're collections of individual tools, when the research suggests they behave more like social systems. Nobody has a security playbook for those yet.

title: CEO's AI clone faces Wall Street
content:
Halfway through Customers Bank's first-quarter earnings call last Friday, CEO Sam Sidhu told analysts something that made at least one of them need a minute. The prepared remarks they'd been listening to for roughly 30 minutes weren't delivered by him. They were delivered by his AI clone.

"I'm still recovering from the shock," Kelly Motta, managing director of equity research at Keefe Bruyette & Woods, said on the call. The bank's CFO Mark McCollom kept it simpler: "Was me the whole time."

The stunt was deliberate. Customers Bank had just signed a multiyear partnership with OpenAI to embed the company's engineers directly inside the bank and automate lending, onboarding and payments. Sidhu, who took over as CEO in January after a planned transition from his father, used the clone as a live product demo of what the bank is building. Four months into the job and his first major act was proving in front of Wall Street that the technology could stand in for him without anyone noticing.

The financials make the showmanship harder to dismiss. According to the bank's Q1 2026 earnings, Customers Bank's efficiency ratio, which measures how much it costs to earn a dollar of revenue, dropped from 52.94% to 49.68% in a year. For a bank, a 326 basis point improvement in a single year is significant. Net income jumped from $9.5 million to $69.7 million. Revenue grew 58% year-over-year while core earnings increased by 28%.

Sidhu told CNBC the bank already uses AI to write about half its internal code and has saved roughly 28,000 work hours, the equivalent of about 15 full-time employees. The next phase targets compressing commercial loan closings from 30 to 45 days down to around seven, and cutting complex account openings from over a day to under 20 minutes. AI agents for lending, deposits and payments are expected to roll out over the next six to 12 months.

Most companies that announce AI partnerships are buying a software license. Customers Bank and OpenAI are co-building. "We're going to be co-creating enterprise solutions they could potentially sell to other banks in the future," Sidhu told CNBC. So the bank becomes a development partner rather than a customer. OpenAI gets real-world use cases inside a regulated institution, and Customers Bank gets tools designed for its specific workflows. "We expect a fundamental re-engineering of how Customers Bank operates," Sidhu said in the announcement.

Sidhu argues that a $26 billion regional bank can move faster on this than the megabanks because places like JPMorgan carry far more regulatory complexity around AI implementation. And there's a telling detail in the expense breakdown that suggests the strategy is more nuanced than just automating everyone out of a job: salaries went up 20% year over year because the bank is hiring more bankers, but technology spending barely moved. They're hiring humans and arming them with AI.

That said, Sidhu used an earnings call as a live AI demo at a time when regulators are actively questioning whether AI-generated executive communications need new rules. Former SEC Chair Gary Gensler warned that companies making AI claims need "a reasonable basis" for them and explicitly flagged "AI washing" as a potential securities law violation. Sidhu may be ahead of the technology curve, but the disclosure rules haven't caught up yet.

Into the Valley

The clone stunt only works once as a surprise. Nobody's going to be shocked by it next quarter. What could work repeatedly is the operating model underneath it, where a mid-size bank embeds the AI vendor's engineers directly into the institution and co-builds products both sides can sell. If that structure delivers at Customers Bank, OpenAI has a template it can run at dozens of other banks, and Sidhu's $26 billion lender becomes the reference customer for an entire industry's transformation. That's a much bigger bet than cloning yourself for 30 minutes, and it's the one that actually tells us something.

  • AI already writes about half the bank's internal code and has saved roughly 28,000 work hours — the equivalent of about 15 full-time employees

Most companies that announce AI partnerships are buying a software license. Customers Bank and OpenAI are co-building. "We're going to be co-creating enterprise solutions they could potentially sell to other banks in the future," Sidhu told CNBC. OpenAI gets real-world use cases inside a regulated institution; Customers Bank gets tools designed for its specific workflows. Next up: AI agents for lending, deposits and payments over the next six to 12 months, with a goal of compressing commercial loan closings from 30–45 days down to about seven.

There's also a telling detail in the expense breakdown that suggests this isn't just an automation play: salaries went up 20% year over year because the bank is hiring more bankers, while technology spending barely moved. They're hiring humans and arming them with AI. Sidhu argues a $26 billion regional bank can move faster on this than the megabanks because places like JPMorgan carry far more regulatory complexity around AI implementation.

That said, using an earnings call as a live AI demo raises questions. Former SEC Chair Gary Gensler has warned that companies making AI claims need "a reasonable basis" for them, explicitly flagging "AI washing" as a potential securities law violation. Sidhu may be ahead of the technology curve, but the disclosure rules haven't caught up yet.

Into the Valley

The clone stunt only works once as a surprise. Nobody's going to be shocked by it next quarter. What could work repeatedly is the operating model underneath it, where a mid-size bank embeds the AI vendor's engineers directly into the institution and co-builds products both sides can sell. If that structure delivers at Customers Bank, OpenAI has a template it can run at dozens of other banks, and Sidhu's $26 billion lender becomes the reference customer for an entire industry's transformation. That's a much bigger bet than cloning yourself for 30 minutes, and it's the one that actually tells us something.
author: Thorium Valley

title: He manages more than 30 AI agents and can't write a line of code
content:
Andy Cabasso can't code. He'll be the first to tell you. But every morning when he opens his laptop at ClickUp, more than 30 AI agents are already waiting with finished work.

Cabasso runs growth operations at the productivity platform and over the past year has built a fleet of AI agents that handle the stuff he used to spend hours doing by hand. He told Business Insider he uses about 15 to 20 of them on any given day:

  • Campaign analytics agent: Pulls performance data from the outbound platform, compares campaigns against each other, recommends changes, and then implements those changes itself
  • Meeting transcript agent: Reviews his recordings and surfaces key takeaways
  • Follow-up agent: Automatically creates tasks after meetings
  • Scheduling agent: Looks at his calendar and task list each morning and plans out his day

Worth mentioning early: Cabasso works at a company that builds and sells AI agent tools. ClickUp offers a no-code agent builder that lets non-technical people create agents without engineering help, and the company actively encouraged employees to adopt them in daily workflows. That's a pretty significant home-court advantage, and the story should be read with that in mind.

Still, what happened to his actual job is the part worth paying attention to. A year ago his mornings looked like a lot of people's mornings: pulling reports, building tables, organizing data. Now the reports are done before he arrives. He spends most of his day reviewing agent outputs, adjusting prompts when something breaks, and figuring out how agents can hand work off to each other without creating a mess.

"It's a new kind of job, and I don't think my role is disappearing," he told Business Insider. "It's just shape-shifting."

Some of that shape-shifting has been surprisingly creative. Cabasso gives certain agents fictional personalities because he found that default AI outputs tend to be, in his words, "bland" or "sycophantic." So one agent thinks it's on the USS Enterprise from Star Trek. His habit-tracking agent has the personality of Matt Foley, the motivational speaker from SNL. A vendor negotiation agent channels FBI hostage negotiator Chris Voss. Agents modeled on personalities with relevant expertise actually approach problems differently, which produces better output for certain tasks. Not all of them stuck, though. A Yoda-voiced agent got retired fast because the inverted sentence structure made every response annoying to parse.

His agent count grew incrementally. The scheduling agent was his first. He posted on LinkedIn after building 19 in 60 days and has nearly doubled that since. Each new agent only went live after the previous ones proved reliable enough to trust. He scoped every one to a single workflow rather than trying to build some all-purpose super-agent, and he reviews output daily the same way you'd review a new employee's work.

That puts him pretty far ahead of most. ClickUp's own research found 62% of people say agents don't live up to the hype and 30% say their biggest frustration is agents that "sound confident but get things wrong." Dr. Jason Wingard wrote in Forbes that every middle manager "is on a clock" to either evolve into what he calls a "Judgment Manager" or get replaced by the agents they're supposed to oversee. Cabasso looks like proof of the first option, though with a very favorable testing environment.

"I don't know what things will look like in a few years," Cabasso said, "but I will likely create more agents and will have more layers of orchestration with agents running other agents in a very fixed scope with very specific instructions."

Into the Valley

Cabasso had every advantage in making this work: ClickUp's no-code tools, a company culture that encouraged experimentation, and more than 30 chances to figure it out. But the reason it worked is that he managed agents the way you'd manage people. Scoped roles, daily reviews, one new hire at a time. If the most valuable AI skill of the next few years turns out to be plain old management, that's going to be a strange pill for the tech industry to swallow.

title: BCG says 'start the pump' on AI tokens. Its own research disagrees.
content:
A senior BCG executive said companies need to "start the pump" on AI usage, warning that holding back puts engineers "on the trajectory to become obsolete." Companies took the advice, and some of them have gotten pretty weird about it.

Sylvain Duranton runs BCG X, the firm's tech and design division. He told Business Insider that companies need to dramatically increase their AI token spending. Tokens are the units that AI models use to process text, and companies get billed based on how many their employees consume. Duranton's argument is that tokens are becoming the next competitive resource after people and capital.

The mandate is already showing up inside companies, and some of the implementations are revealing.

  • Meta built an internal leaderboard called "Claudeonomics" that tracked the top 250 power users out of more than 85,000 employees, with titles like "Token Legend," "Session Immortal," and "Cache Wizard." The company collectively burned through 60.2 trillion tokens in a single 30-day window.
  • Salesforce created a desktop widget that updates individual token spend every 15 minutes, with minimum spending targets of $100 a month on Claude Code and $70 on Cursor. Any employee can look up any colleague's number.
  • Software engineering blogger Gergely Orosz noted on X that AI usage is now part of Meta's performance evaluations, driving employees to hit targets simply to "get that exceeds expectations (or above) rating."

All of these systems assume the same thing, that more tokens means better work. The early evidence says that's wrong. A randomized controlled trial from METR, a safety research organization, found that developers using AI tools actually took 19% longer to complete tasks than those working without them. And even after seeing the results, those same developers still believed AI had made them about 20% faster. As one engineering leader told Abi Noda, CEO of developer productivity platform DX: "My CEO, our executives, are expecting astronomical gains because there's so much hype about AI in the media, but that's not what we're seeing on the ground." Every incentive being built around token usage right now is rewarding a feeling of productivity that the data doesn't support.

Duranton seemed to sense the tension himself. In the same conversation he said "if everyone is burning tokens to write poems and do pictures, there's not much benefit" and that "token consumption alone doesn't reveal what an employee is doing." That's a significant walk-back from the person who just urged companies to "start the pump" on token spending. BCG's own published research from late 2025 found that more than 85% of employees were stuck in low-value AI usage, concluding that "adoption quality is the goal, not adoption rate." The same firm is saying two very different things.

The cost of following the volume playbook is getting harder to ignore. Some developers at a large fintech have driven token spend "off the charts" on tools like Claude Code, fundamentally altering the cost models for internal tooling. A small AI startup saw per-developer spend jump from $200 a month to $3,000 in six months. Duranton described the friction directly, with CFOs watching AI budgets explode while CIOs insist the spending is necessary.

For contrast, AT&T processes 27 billion tokens a day and built its entire strategy around running cheaper, efficient models rather than burning through frontier ones. One of the largest token consumers in the country got there by spending less per token, not more.

Into the Valley

BCG published research saying most AI usage is low-value and that quality matters more than volume. Then one of its senior partners went on the record saying companies need to "start the pump" on AI token spending. Both can't be right, and the early data sides with the research paper. Token consumption is becoming the new "hours at your desk," something visible that feels like productivity without actually proving it. The companies handing out "Cache Wizard" badges are measuring the wrong thing.

title: Google's AI search is crushing publisher traffic
content:
Tech publishers just lost more than half their Google traffic.

A Growtika analysis tracking 10 major tech publications found that their combined US traffic from Google dropped 58% between early 2024 and January 2026, falling from 112 million organic visits per month to 47 million. Some sites practically disappeared:

  • Digital Trends: down 97%, from 8.5 million monthly visits to 265,000
  • ZDNet: down 90%
  • The Verge: down 85%
  • TechRadar: down 74%

This goes beyond tech. NerdWallet, a publicly traded personal finance site, saw a 73% decline over the same period. Healthline lost 55 million monthly visits on its own, more traffic than all 10 tech publishers currently have combined. Separate Chartbeat data analyzed by ALM tells a similar story for smaller publishers, with roughly a 60% drop in search traffic.

The cause is Google's AI Overviews, the AI-generated summaries that now sit at the top of search results and answer your question before you ever need to click a link. A Seer Interactive study of over 311 million impressions found that when a publisher isn't cited in an AI Overview, their click-through rate drops 67%. Even publishers that are cited still see 38% fewer clicks compared to results without an AI Overview at all.

Publishers have tried to fight back by blocking AI bots from scraping their content. About 75% of top publishers have done so at various points since mid-2023. But blocking actually makes things worse: those publishers saw a 7% decline in weekly visits because they lost the brand exposure that comes from being referenced in AI-generated answers. It's a lose-lose. Block the bots and lose visibility, or let them scrape your work and watch it get summarized above your own link.

"The fundamental business model of the internet is going to break down if AI tools don't generate traffic to original sources," Matthew Prince, CEO of Cloudflare, said at Web Summit.

Google has called the Growtika analysis "fundamentally flawed," citing a small sample size and lack of seasonal adjustment. There are some signs that the worst may be leveling off. Seer Interactive found that organic click-through rates on AI Overview queries climbed from 1.3% in December 2025 to 2.4% by February 2026. That's still well below where things stood before AI Overviews existed, but the freefall has at least flattened.

Regulators are starting to notice. The UK's Competition and Markets Authority proposed measures in January to give publishers more control over how their content appears in Google search. But regulation and Big Tech move at very different speeds, and by the time any ruling survives the appeals process, the damage will already be done.

Into the Valley

Google built one of the most profitable businesses in history by sending people to websites. AI Overviews are breaking that loop, and publishers have nowhere good to turn: blocking bots costs them visibility, and regulators won't move fast enough to matter. If the companies summarizing the web can't figure out how to sustain the people creating the content they depend on, there eventually won't be much left worth summarizing.

title: Microsoft charges more for AI fewer people trust
content:
Microsoft is raising the price of nearly every 365 subscription starting July 1. The pitch is better AI tools. The problem is most people who already have access aren't using them.

Price increases are hitting across the board, bundling Copilot capabilities deeper into the productivity suite that hundreds of millions of workers rely on. The bumps range from 5% to 33%:

  • Business Basic: $6 to $7/user/month (16%)
  • Business Standard: $12.50 to $14 (12%)
  • Enterprise E3: $36 to $39 (8%)
  • Enterprise E5: $57 to $60 (5%)
  • Frontline F1: $2.25 to $3 (33%)
  • Frontline F3: $8 to $10 (25%)

Microsoft also introduced a new Enterprise E7 tier at about $99 per user per month, packaging its Agent 365 platform with security and compliance features. Gartner's initial assessment was not kind, calling Agent 365 "a work in progress with limited net new functionality to justify its $15 price point."

Then there's GitHub Copilot, which shifts to usage-based pricing on June 1. Developers will pay based on what they actually consume rather than a flat monthly fee. It's the one pricing change that could benefit lighter users, but it also signals Microsoft sees metered AI billing as the future.

Three moves, same bet. Microsoft is making AI the cost of doing business whether you asked for it or not.

That bet would be easier to justify if people were actually using the AI. A Recon Analytics survey of over 150,000 US respondents found that only about 36% of employees with Copilot access use it regularly. ChatGPT sees an 83% conversion rate among workers who have access, more than double.

Copilot's paid subscriber market share has been shrinking too, falling from roughly 19% last July to about 11.5% by January, according to the same data. Google's Gemini passed it quietly in late November, now holding nearly 16% of paid AI subscribers.

The trust numbers are rougher. Recon Analytics tracked Copilot's accuracy Net Promoter Score across three points: -3.5 last summer, deteriorating to -24.1 by September, then partially recovering to -19.8 in January. Nearly half of people who tried Copilot and stopped say they did so because they don't trust the answers it gives them.

The cost pressures behind these increases aren't going away either. Nik Kale, a principal engineer at Cisco, said the price bumps aren't "a temporary spike" but "the beginning of a new price baseline for the AI era," reflecting the real GPU and energy costs behind every AI product on the market.

Nadella's answer, laid out on Microsoft's Q3 earnings call, is that the company is moving toward an "evaluation-based" or "outcome-based" pricing model where customers pay for the value AI agents actually create. CFO Amy Hood said margins on the AI business remain better than during Microsoft's initial cloud transition. Citi analyst Tyler Radke captured the broader mood, calling the quarter "solid execution versus a step change in momentum."

That tension isn't limited to Microsoft. As the LA Times noted, the trillion-dollar question across Big Tech right now is whether all this AI spending is actually producing returns, or whether companies are building expensive foundations for demand that hasn't fully shown up.

Into the Valley

Microsoft wants to eventually be the company that charges you based on what AI actually does for you. That's an attractive pitch. But right now, the company is doing the opposite — raising prices on a product most customers either ignore or actively distrust. The bet is that switching away from 365 is painful enough to buy Copilot time to improve. Every price increase before it earns that trust makes the "should we switch?" conversation a little louder, and Google is making sure those conversations have somewhere to go.

title: FlightStory spent $20K on an AI competition. It found $1.18M.
content:
Most companies are struggling to get any return from AI. Steven Bartlett's media company found $1.18 million in savings by turning adoption into a game.

FlightStory, the company behind Bartlett's media and investment portfolio, ran a 60-day internal competition last year. Teams across the company competed to find the best ways to use AI agents in their daily work. The winning team took home a $20,000 prize.

Across the company, employees identified $1,180,232 in efficiency savings and unlocked more than 65,000 hours of productivity. The winning pre-production team built tools and agents that replaced or improved nearly every part of their workflow. Other teams created an AI-powered ad pitch tool that cut turnaround from three days to hours, a Spanish translation system that generated $200,000 in new YouTube ad revenue, and an AI-animated kids show.

Isaac Martin, FlightStory's Director of Innovation, called it "a scrappy test for us to very much dive into that space and just see what worked, and see what we could do in a short space of time."

None of these ideas came from consultants or leadership mandates. They came from employees who knew firsthand which parts of their day were slow or repetitive enough to hand off to an AI agent. Bartlett said the competition was about "inspiring a mindset shift" and "going on the journey of change together."

Most organizations are trying to close the AI gap from the opposite direction, and it's not going well. A Cisco study of over 2,500 CEOs found that 97% plan to integrate AI, but only 1.7% feel fully prepared. The tools and budgets are there. The problem is getting people to actually use them.

FlightStory isn't alone in betting that competitions can bridge that gap. Spectrum ran a hackathon where employees built a production-ready feature in under three days that would normally take six to eight weeks. Zapier now requires every new hire to demonstrate AI fluency before they walk in the door. Internal AI competitions are quietly becoming standard practice.

Shopify CEO Tobi Lütke took a different angle earlier this year, sending a company-wide memo telling teams to prove they can't get the job done with AI before asking for more headcount. He pushed managers to ask themselves: "What would this area look like if autonomous AI agents were already part of the team?"

FlightStory says its broader AI push has increased average revenue per person by 60% over two years. The competition was the latest chapter in that shift, but $1.18 million from a $20,000 investment makes the math hard to argue with.

Into the Valley

The most expensive AI strategy is one nobody uses. FlightStory's competition worked not because the tools were groundbreaking but because employees had a reason to actually try them. That's the step most companies skip. They sign the enterprise license, send the all-staff email, and six months later wonder why adoption never took off. Expect this playbook to spread. A $20,000 prize that surfaces a million dollars in savings is the kind of math that gets a CFO's attention, and the hard part of AI adoption was never the technology. It was giving people a reason to go looking.

title: Microsoft's OpenAI exclusivity backfired.
content:
Microsoft had OpenAI all to itself. That's over now.

On Tuesday, OpenAI announced that its models, Codex, and managed agents are now available on Amazon Web Services through Amazon Bedrock. For years, Microsoft held exclusive cloud distribution rights to OpenAI's models through Azure. A restructured agreement made that license non-exclusive, freeing OpenAI to sell wherever its customers already are.

Amazon isn't treating this as a test run. The company is investing $50 billion in OpenAI, $15 billion upfront with $35 billion conditional, while expanding an existing cloud agreement by $100 billion over eight years. OpenAI also committed to roughly 2 gigawatts of AWS compute capacity running on Amazon's custom Trainium chips.

The Azure exclusivity had been quietly costing OpenAI customers. During the years OpenAI was locked to Microsoft's cloud, its enterprise market share dropped from around 50% to roughly 27%, according to Menlo Ventures' year-end enterprise AI report. Anthropic, which has been available on AWS from day one, climbed from about 12% to 40% over the same period. The arrangement that was supposed to be an advantage pushed enterprise buyers straight to the competition.

AWS CEO Matt Garman was blunt about the dynamic during a keynote at AWS's San Francisco event. Enterprises already had their production apps, their data, and their security infrastructure in AWS. "We've forced them for the last couple of years, to get great OpenAI models, to go to other places," he said.

Developers noticed. Chris Alexander, an engineer, posted on X that Azure's OpenAI endpoints were "so unreliable, we mostly just hit you all directly." When your distribution partner is driving customers to skip the middleman, the partnership has a problem.

OpenAI's revenue chief, Denise Dresser, acknowledged as much internally. In a memo to staff, she called the Microsoft partnership "foundational" but said it had "limited our ability to meet enterprises where they are," adding that for many customers, that now means Bedrock.

Microsoft framed the change as business as usual. A joint statement from February said partnerships like the Amazon deal "were always contemplated under our agreements." Wall Street read it differently, with UBS analysts writing that Microsoft "appears to have made more concessions than gains." Microsoft's cloud revenue this quarter actually beat expectations — Azure grew 40%, clearing the roughly 39% consensus — but the market wanted acceleration it didn't get, and shares dropped 2% in extended trading.

Into the Valley

Anthropic didn't win enterprise market share on model quality alone. It won by being available where companies already worked. OpenAI just confirmed, with a $50 billion handshake, that distribution matters at least as much as intelligence itself — because OpenAI is not going to sit back and watch this happen quietly.
