title: Snap's $400M Perplexity deal died after user testing flopped
content:
Perplexity was willing to pay $400 million to be inside Snapchat. Users weren't interested.

Snap disclosed during Q1 earnings on Wednesday that its partnership with AI search startup Perplexity has "amicably ended." The deal, announced last November, would have embedded Perplexity's search engine directly into Snapchat's messaging experience. Under the terms, Perplexity was obligated to pay Snap $400 million in cash and equity over a year, buying distribution to Snap's 483 million daily active users.

It lasted less than five months. By February, Snap said the two companies had "yet to mutually agree on a path to a broader roll out," only three months into testing. A Perplexity spokesperson told Engadget that the original implementation wasn't the right fit for either company's product goals.

Snap already had a conversational AI product that people used regularly. Over half a billion Snapchatters have messaged My AI since launch, and users sent more than 950 billion chats on the platform in Q1 alone. A search engine inside a messaging app built around casual conversation never quite fit, and testing proved it.

Snap launched AI Sponsored Snaps on April 28, its own bet on making money from AI conversations. The format lets brands show up inside My AI chats when a topic is relevant, and Snap's existing Sponsored Snaps format shows click-through rates 226% higher than standard Snap ads. "Conversation is becoming the most valuable real estate in advertising," said Ajit Mohan, Snap's chief business officer.

Perplexity has gone the other way. The company walked away from advertising altogether in February, telling reporters that ads undermined users' trust. Executives said the company doesn't track monthly active users because "we're not actually on a mission to get as many users as possible." Perplexity is now chasing what it describes as a "boutique" audience of people making "GDP-moving decisions," funded by enterprise subscriptions and publisher revenue.

The split comes during a tough stretch for Snap. The company laid off about 1,000 employees in April, roughly 16% of its workforce, while targeting more than $500 million in annualized cost cuts. CEO Evan Spiegel pointed to a return to user growth and accelerating revenue on the earnings call, but losing a $400 million revenue line while also cutting headcount adds real pressure.

Our Valley View

You can't buy product-market fit, even for $400 million. Both companies walked away from this deal and landed on strategies that actually suit them, which tells you how little they needed each other in the first place. As AI startups everywhere scramble to prove a business model, expect more expensive breakups like this one. The partnerships that survive will be the ones where users actually wanted the product, not the ones where the term sheet looked impressive.

title: Coding is eating every other AI use case alive
content:
Ask any CEO what their company uses AI for and you'll hear the same answer on repeat.

Andreessen Horowitz just published the clearest picture yet of where big companies are actually spending money on AI. The headline number: coding is the dominant enterprise use case by nearly an order of magnitude. That's roughly 10 times more enterprise AI activity going toward writing and reviewing code than toward the next closest category.

And we're still early. Only about 29% of Fortune 500 companies are live, paying customers of a leading AI startup, according to the data. Among those that have, coding dwarfs everything else, with customer support and search as distant runners-up.

The reason coding pulled so far ahead is straightforward. Code is the one domain where you can verify AI's output instantly. Run it, see if it breaks. That feedback loop lets models improve faster here than in more subjective fields like strategy or creative work. It also means AI-generated code has become something bigger than software development, because anything you can describe clearly enough can now be built by a model.

Which is partly why bragging about AI-generated code has become the CEO flex of 2026. Spotify's top developers haven't handwritten a line of code since December. Airbnb says AI coauthors nearly 60% of its new code. These aren't pilots. They're the new operating default.

Steve Yegge, a software engineering veteran with over 30 years across Amazon, Google and Grab, described it this way: "Every company has a dial that they turn from zero to a hundred" on the percentage of engineering staff that can be let go. That dial only turns in one direction. He also pointed out that the gap between major model releases has compressed from about eight months to four, so companies that wait aren't just falling behind. They're falling behind faster.

Other verticals are picking up, though:

  • Legal: Harvey, which we covered earlier this week, secured $200 million in new funding and raised at an $11 billion valuation. Sequoia's Pat Grady called it "the platform on which legal work runs."
  • Customer support: The outsourcing market represents over $300 billion in annual spend, and AI startups are targeting it with reported resolution rates above 80%.
  • Accounting and auditing: Model capabilities here jumped nearly 20% in just four months, one of the fastest-improving non-coding domains.

These categories are growing fast, but they trail coding by a wide margin. Alex Immerman and Santiago Rodriguez at a16z argue that better models won't shrink the software industry. They'll expand it, "because the hard part was never raw intelligence. It was knowing what to do with it."

Our Valley View

Coding became AI's breakout use case because verification is built in. You don't need a committee to evaluate the output, you just run it. Most white-collar work doesn't have that luxury, which is why every other vertical is still playing catch-up. The industries that figure out their own version of instant verification, whether that's tracking case outcomes in legal or resolution rates in support, will be the next to take off. As a16z's Anish Acharya put it: "The world is still short software." Coding has the receipts. Everything else is still making promises.
